card: Husband goes silent after an argument: why, and what helps
title: Husband goes silent after an argument: what to do next
desc: Silence after a fight rarely means he stopped caring. Usually it is overwhelm or self-defense. What the quiet really means and how to start talking again.
h1: Husband goes silent after an argument: why he does it and how to start talking again
alt: Two people sitting back to back, each with their own phone and their own chat bubble
tldr: Silence almost never means "I don't care." Usually it means he is overwhelmed, or afraid of making it worse.
Pushing gets you nowhere. What works is a pause with the door left open, and a first message with no blame in it.
Past two or three days, the quiet stops being a pause and starts being a punishment. That is a separate problem.
body:
Day two of the quiet. He walks past, answers in one word, stays on his phone longer than usual. You have already run thirty versions of the conversation in your head and a hundred versions of the hurt. When a husband goes silent after an argument, it can feel worse than the argument did. At least shouting tells you what is happening.

First, the part that matters most. Silence almost never means "I don't care." It has other causes, and which one you are dealing with changes what you should do next.

What is actually behind the silence

He is flooded

The most common reason has a dull physical explanation. In a fight, a lot of men's heart rates spike faster and settle slower. A brain in that state doesn't hold conversations, it defends. Silence then isn't a weapon, it's a fire exit: I can't take this much heat, so I'm shutting down before I say something worse. Researchers who study couples noticed a long time ago that men stonewall like this far more often than women do.

He is scared of making it worse

Plenty of people grew up learning that saying anything only turns the volume up. Someone like that goes quiet not against you but out of helplessness. He has no script for a conversation that doesn't end in a second fight.

A hurt that never got words

Sometimes he thinks he is the injured one and is waiting for the apology from you. Saying that out loud feels awkward, or pride won't let him, so the hurt comes out the only way it can: as distance.

Silence used as leverage

This one is a different story. If the quiet switches on regularly and lifts at the exact moment you come back ready to make up on any terms, silence is being used to steer you. Telling the two apart is simple. A flooded person thaws slowly on his own. Someone using it holds the pause until you give in.
chat: He hasn't said a word in two days. I can't tell if he's hurt or if he just doesn't care.

It sounds like the silence frightens you more than the fight did: you fill it in with the worst version. From the way he shut down right after the shouting, this looks more like overwhelm than indifference.
When you're ready, send him one line with no question and no blame in it. Something like: I don't want to fight. Can we talk when you're up for it?

Tell Mediator what happened. It helps you separate what actually hurt from what you are filling in on your own, work out what you want to say, and hands you a first line to open with. Walking into the conversation with that is far easier than walking in with two days of silence. The first analysis is free.
after:
What to do when your husband goes silent after an argument

Give him air, but leave the door open

"Talk to me right now" doesn't work. It sinks a flooded person deeper. What works is a pause with the door left open: "I can see you're not up for talking. I'm ready to listen whenever you are. It matters to me." Then actually wait, instead of checking on him every half hour.

Start small, and not with a complaint

The first contact after silence should be ordinary and short. Tea, "how are you doing," something funny off your phone. That isn't surrender, it's a bridge. The real conversation goes easier after five minutes of normal life.

Talk about you, not about his silence

"There you go again, sitting there like a statue" will extend the quiet, guaranteed. Another version leaves him room to come out without losing face: "The silence is hard on me, I start imagining the worst. Help me understand what's going on with you."

A line you can open with

"The silence is hard on me, I start imagining the worst. I'm not pushing. Just tell me when you can talk."

Offer an easier format

Some men find it simpler to write than to speak. A text, a voice note, a sticky note on the fridge. That isn't a lesser version of the conversation, it's the start of it.

What not to do

  • Don't lay siege with questions. The twentieth "why won't you say anything" lands like twenty knocks on a closed door.
  • Don't answer silence with silence. Two people not talking isn't a pause any more, it's a cold war, and those take twice as long to end.
  • Don't hand down verdicts into the quiet: "he's not talking, so he must be done with me." A story you build in a vacuum is always scarier than the truth.

If it happens every single week

One stretch of silence after a hard fight is fixed by the steps above. Silence as a weekly ritual is usually a symptom of a deeper groove, and there is a separate piece on that: why couples keep fighting over small things. And if the quiet is there to make sure you always give in first, it is fairer to call that what it is and take it to a professional.
faq: How long is it normal to go without talking after a fight?

Anywhere from a couple of hours to a day. That is roughly what a nervous system needs to genuinely cool down. Past two or three days, the silence stops being a pause and starts doing damage of its own.
Should I be the one to text him first?

If the only thing stopping you is the principle of it, then text him. One calm message with no reproach in it costs your pride nothing and often lifts the whole siege: "I don't want to fight. Can we talk when you're ready?"
Is the silent treatment a form of manipulation?

Not always. Most of the time it is overwhelm, and it thaws on its own within a day or two. It turns into control when it is used on repeat and always ends the moment you apologize for everything. If that is the pattern, the silence is the problem, not the fight.

card: Constantly fighting over small things: what it really means
title: Constantly fighting over small things: what it means
desc: When a couple fights about dishes, socks and tone of voice every week, it is not about the dishes. How to find the real topic underneath and break the cycle.
h1: Constantly fighting over small things: what it really means and how to break the cycle
alt: A person calmly untangling a ball of thread that ends in a small heart
tldr: Small fights are a lightning rod. One big topic is hiding behind the dishes and the socks.
The cycle does not break on its own, because a truce without a conversation leaves the topic exactly where it was.
Three moves break it: name the groove out loud, discuss the real topic in peacetime, and repair the same day.
body:
Monday: a fight about the dishes. Wednesday: about the tone of voice in a "sure." Saturday: about which route to take to his mother's. From the outside, constantly fighting over small things looks like the two of you are just difficult. From the inside it feels worse, like the relationship turned into a minefield where anything can go off.

Here is the good news. Couples who are constantly fighting over small things are almost never fighting about the small things. Here is the bad news. That means there is one big topic you are walking around, and it seeps out through every crack.

The small thing is a lightning rod

Socks on the floor cannot cause a storm week after week. The storm comes from somewhere else. Usually one of these is sitting underneath a run of little fights:

  • An unfair split at home. One of you carries more and feels like staff instead of a partner.
  • Not enough attention. A fight becomes the only reliable way to get a strong reaction out of the other person. Any reaction.
  • Exhaustion nobody has admitted. You are both wrung out by work or kids, and neither of you has anything left for gentleness.
  • An old hurt that never got said. It was forgiven out loud but not for real, and now it tints every conversation.
  • Different ideas about the future, about money, or about where the line with family is, and all of them feel too big to raise directly.

The test is simple. Think of your last three fights and ask yourself what your feeling had in common each time. If it is "I'm not being heard" or "I'm the only one trying here" every time, you have found the real topic.

A line you can open with

"I don't think we're fighting about the dishes. Can we sit down some quiet evening and look at what's under it? I'm not blaming you, I honestly want to know how it looks from your side."

Why fighting over small things turns into a cycle

Repeat fights run in a worn groove. Same trigger, same lines, same door slam, same sticky truce a day later with nothing settled. Psychologists call it a cycle, and every lap wears the groove a little deeper, which makes climbing out harder each time.

A truce with no conversation in it is the fuel. The fight gets muffled, the topic stays. A few days later it needs a fresh excuse, and the dishes are always within reach.
chat: We fought about who takes out the trash. Again. Third time this week.
The trash looks like the excuse here. When you write "me again," the anger isn't at the bag. It's at the fact that the house runs on you and nobody notices.
Last time the topic was the same, only it was the dishes. This week, try naming it out loud: not "you didn't take it out," but "I feel alone carrying all of this."
try: Mediator asks the questions that are hard to reach on your own: what keeps repeating, what you feel every time, what you are missing. It also remembers the topics of your earlier sessions and will tell you when a fight is going in circles. The first analysis is free.
after:
Three moves that break the cycle

1. Name the groove out loud

Here is a strong move almost nobody tries: talk about the pattern instead of the last fight. "Look, we've been fighting about nothing every week for three months. I don't think it's about the nothing. Let's find what's under it." That moves the two of you from opponents to two people studying the same problem.

2. Talk about the real topic in peacetime

The big topic cannot be discussed mid-battle. Pick a calm evening, no phones, and don't open with "we need to have a serious talk." One honest run at it is enough: "I don't think I'm angry about the dishes. I think I'm angry that I feel alone in running our life. Tell me how it looks from where you're standing."

3. Repair fast

Strong couples don't fight less than shaky ones. The difference is the speed of the repair. They apologize and talk it through the same day, while the hurt is still soft. There is a step-by-step version of that in our piece on how to make up after a big fight.

When small fights stop being small

If contempt has joined the frequency, or put-downs in front of other people, or a fear of speaking up at home, this is no longer two people learning to live together. That kind of thing doesn't get fixed alone or by a bot. You want a couples therapist. It isn't a defeat, it's an ordinary repair job, just with someone who does it for a living.
faq: Is it normal for couples to argue this much?
Yes. The only people who never argue are strangers and couples where one person gave up a while ago. The question is never whether you fight, it is whether you repair afterward.
Why do we keep fighting about the same thing over and over?

Because the fight keeps ending without the topic being settled. The tension drops, the reason stays, and a few days later it finds a new trigger. The loop breaks when you talk about the real topic during a calm stretch, not during the fight.
We make up in bed and it seems to work. Why does it keep coming back?
Because closeness takes the tension down but doesn't answer the question that created it. It is a painkiller, not a treatment. It works alongside the conversation, not instead of it.

card: How to make up after a big fight: a step-by-step plan
title: How to make up after a big fight: step-by-step plan
desc: The first day after a fight decides more than a week of silence. Step-by-step: how to cool down, name what hurt, and open the talk without a second fight.
h1: How to make up after a big fight: step by step, before the hurt sets
alt: Two people tying a ribbon around a closed book, with two cups of tea beside them
tldr: The first day after a fight decides more than a week of silence, because the hurt is still soft.
The order matters: cool the body down, name what hurt, open with yourself, then hear their version.
Twenty minutes in is too early to make up. A week later it is already hard.
body:
A fresh hurt behaves like cement. For the first day it is still wet: you can work with it, talk it through, clear it away. After a week of silence it sets, and every fight after that lands on top of the old one. Which is why the best time to make up after a big fight is the first day or two, the stretch couples therapists call the repair window.

At the same time, trying to make up after a big fight in the first twenty minutes is its own mistake. Here is what to do and in what order.

Step 1. Cool the body first, the head second

During a serious fight the pulse climbs past a hundred and the brain flips into defense. In that state a person physically cannot listen. Everything the other one says sounds like an attack. The psychologist John Gottman, who spent forty years watching couples in a lab, called it flooding.

So the first move is boring: a break of at least twenty minutes. Go for a walk, take a shower, do the dishes. One rule matters. A break is announced, not slammed. "I can't talk about this calmly right now, let's come back to it in an hour" stings much less than a silent exit, which your partner will read as a punishment.

Step 2. Work out what actually hurt

A fight is almost never about what it is officially about. A blow-up over unwashed dishes is usually not about dishes, it is about "I carry everything and nobody values it." Shouting about being late is not about the minutes, it is about "your stuff always comes before me."

Until you have named the real reason to yourself, making up is risky. You will make up about the dishes, and the hurt about not being valued will still be sitting there, ready to go off next week. Ask yourself three questions, and it is better to write the answers down:

  • What actually happened, with every "always" and "never" taken out?
  • What did I feel in that moment: anger, hurt, fear, loneliness?
  • What was I really missing: attention, respect, help, some certainty?

On paper this works better than in your head. Thoughts on a loop just grind the same hurt down. A written sentence forces it into a shape you can look at.
chat: We screamed at each other about vacation plans and now neither of us is talking. I don't know where to start.
From what you've written, the sting isn't the destination. It's that the decision got made without you. That's about not being counted, and it's the more honest place to start.
Your first line could be: I lost my temper. It matters to me that we decide things like this together. Will you tell me how you saw it?

after:
Step 3. Open with yourself, not with an accusation

There is a simple pattern here: the way the first three minutes start is the way the whole conversation ends. Opening with "we need to talk about your behavior" guarantees a second fight, because your partner is on defense from the first second.

The other approach, sometimes called a soft start-up, works better. The formula is feeling plus specific situation plus need. Compare:

  • "You're always late, you clearly don't care about me" becomes "It hurt to sit there waiting last night. I need to feel like our plans matter to you."
  • "You never help" becomes "I'm worn out and angry. I need help with the house, let's work out how to split it."

The point isn't politeness for its own sake. A sentence that starts with you gives your partner nothing to defend against, and that leaves room for him to actually hear you.

A line you can open with

"Last night hurt, and I want to understand how it looked from your side. Not to fight about it, to figure it out."

Step 4. Let your partner tell their version

The other side always has their own story of the same fight, and it is startlingly unlike yours. As long as each of you holds your version as the only truth, making up stalls. One honest question helps: "tell me how this looked to you." Then listen without interrupting and without assembling your answer while they talk.

What not to do

  • Don't keep score. "Well, back in March you..." turns the talk into a trial, and nobody makes up in a courtroom.
  • Don't generalize. "Always" and "never" are almost always false, and your partner will argue with the wording instead of the point.
  • Don't bring in an audience. Your mother, your best friend and the group chat will hand you more certainty that you're right and take away your chance at peace.
  • Don't demand an ending on the spot. Sometimes you need another day to breathe after the first conversation. That is normal.

When it is too early to make up after a big fight

If the fight involved threats, humiliation or anything physical, this is no longer a question of how to make up. Talk to a real professional, and if you are in danger call your local emergency number (911 in the US). The National Domestic Violence Hotline is free, confidential and open around the clock.
faq: Who should apologize first after a fight?

Whoever gets their strength back first. The first step isn't an admission of guilt, it's an admission that the relationship matters more than being right. The winner in the end isn't the one who waited out the apology, it's the couple.
How long should you go without talking after an argument?
A pause of up to a day usually helps, because people cool off. Silence past two or three days becomes a punishment in itself and winds a new hurt around the old one.
What if he won't talk at all?

Sort out your own half first: what hurt, what you were missing, what you want. A calm person with a clear position lowers someone else's guard faster than any amount of coaxing. We have a separate piece on what silence after a fight usually means.

card: How to apologize so it actually works: the four parts
title: How to apologize so that it actually works: 4 steps
desc: "Sorry, okay?" never works and everyone knows it. What an apology that lands is made of: the specific act, their feelings, no "but," and one real change.
h1: How to apologize so that it actually works
alt: One person holding out a paper heart while the other slowly unclenches their hands
tldr: "Sorry, okay?" makes things worse. What the other person hears is "drop it already."
An apology that works has four parts: the specific act, their feelings, no "but," and one concrete change.
If the apology cost you nothing, it probably will not work.
body:
"Sorry, okay?" Two words that usually leave things worse than they were, because both people hear the same thing in them: drop it already. An apology was technically delivered. What was actually communicated is that your feelings have become annoying. Knowing how to apologize so that it lands is a separate skill from being sorry.

A real apology is built out of more than the word sorry. Not so much more that you can't learn it in one evening.

Why "sorry" on its own bounces off

The person who got hurt doesn't need a word. They need to know three things: that you understand what exactly you did, that you care how it felt for them, and that there is some chance you won't step on the same spot tomorrow. A bare "sorry" answers none of the three, which is why it bounces.

How to apologize so it lands: the four parts

1. Be specific, and drop the "if"

Compare "sorry if I upset you somehow" with "I made a joke about your job in front of your friends last night, and that was humiliating." The first one hands the work back to the injured person: guess what I'm apologizing for, then prove there was something to apologize for. The second shows you understand what you did. The word "if" kills an apology at the starting line.

2. Name what they felt

One sentence does half the work: "I can imagine how that felt." You are not required to agree that their reaction was the only correct one. You are acknowledging that it is real. A hurt that has been seen no longer has to shout.

3. No "but"

"Sorry, but you started it" isn't an apology, it's a counterattack in packaging. Any "but" erases everything in front of it. If you have a grievance of your own, it gets its own conversation. It has no place in this one.

4. One concrete change

"I'll try not to do that again" sounds like a weather forecast. Specifics work: "next time I'm running late, I'll text you right away instead of at midnight." A small promise you can actually keep is worth more than a grand one.

The test is simple. A real apology costs something. Naming a specific act is uncomfortable, changing a habit takes effort. If the apology cost you nothing, it probably isn't working.

An apology that lands

"I made a joke about your job in front of your friends last night. I can imagine how that felt. Next time I'll keep it to myself, and if I really can't, I'll say it to you in private."
chat: I want to apologize, but it always comes out as "sorry if I upset you." And then he's angrier than before.
"If" hands the work back to him: you guess what I'm apologizing for. Let's put the act into words instead. What exactly was said, and when?
Here's a version with no "if": I told your mom you're bad with money. That was humiliating and I'm ashamed of it. I won't talk about our money in front of people again.
try: Mediator has a phrase translator. Write it the way you feel it, anger and all, and it offers calmer versions that keep the meaning. It also helps you unpick the fight itself, so the apology lands on the real hurt instead of the excuse for it. The first analysis is free.
after:
When you both owe an apology

In most fights there are two people at fault, just in different ways. The best apology then is a pair of them: each of you names your own part, with no haggling over whose part was bigger. Whoever cooled off first usually goes first, and that isn't losing, it's being the adult in the room. There is more on how to run the whole conversation after a fight in our step-by-step piece on making up after a big fight.
faq: I apologized and he is still upset. What did I do wrong?

The apology may have landed on the wrong hurt: you apologized for the words, and what got him was something else. Ask him straight out: I want to understand what actually stung. And sometimes a hurt just needs time. Apologies don't work instantly.
Should I apologize if I am right?

Not for your position. For the delivery, sometimes yes. You can make a fair point calmly or at a shout, and a shout stays a shout even when the person shouting is correct. "I still think we need to spend less, but I'm sorry for how I said it last night" is a perfectly consistent sentence.
How do you apologize over text?

The same four parts, only shorter. Name the act, say you can imagine how it felt, skip the "but," and offer one change. Don't send it in the middle of the fight, and don't write three paragraphs. A long text reads like a defense, not an apology.

card: How to fight fair: six rules that protect a relationship
title: How to fight fair: 6 rules that protect a relationship
desc: Strong couples fight as often as everyone else. The difference is how. Six rules for fighting fair: a soft start, no contempt, real pauses and repair afterward.
h1: How to fight fair: 6 rules that keep a conflict from breaking you
alt: Two people at a small table with tea and an hourglass, a smooth thread with no knots running between them
tldr: Happy couples do not fight less often. They fight differently.
Six rules: a soft start, the act not the person, no contempt, a pause with a return, one topic, repair afterward.
Two or more broken rules is fixable with a few weeks of practice.
body:
John Gottman, a psychologist who spent decades watching thousands of couples in his lab, could predict divorce with roughly ninety percent accuracy. The secret turned out to be almost insulting in its simplicity. He wasn't looking at whether a couple fought, he was looking at how. Happy and unhappy couples fight about equally often. What differs is the technique. Put plainly, some couples fight fair and some don't.

Which means fighting is allowed. It is a question of rules. Here are the six that change the most, and together they are most of what it takes to fight fair.

Rule 1. A soft start decides everything

The first three minutes of a conversation almost always tell you how it ends. Opening with an attack ("here you go again") switches your partner into defense, and from there you are not discussing a problem, you are surviving. Opening with yourself leaves the conversation a chance: "I'm upset about yesterday. It's important to me that we talk about it." Same topic, different trajectory.

Rule 2. About the act, not the person

"You forgot to take the trash out" is a complaint about an act, and you can work with it. "You're irresponsible" is a verdict on a person, and all you can do with that is go to war. The moment diagnoses show up in a fight ("you're selfish," "you're just like your mother"), a solvable household question turns into a trial about which of you is a bad human being. Nobody wins those.

Rule 3. Contempt is off limits

Of everything Gottman saw in the lab, the sharpest predictor of divorce wasn't anger. It was contempt: the eye roll, the smirk, the sarcasm, the mimicking. Anger says "what you did hurt me." Contempt says "you're worthless." The first is treatable with a conversation, the second eats a relationship like rust. If you catch yourself smirking, stop the fight right there. The topic can wait.

Rule 4. Pause when you boil over, and promise to come back

When your pulse is through the roof and you want to shout, continuing is pointless. In that state nobody hears anybody. A proper pause sounds like this: "I'm boiling over and I don't want to say something I'll regret. Twenty minutes, then we finish this." An improper one is a silent door slam. The first calms things down, the second punishes. And you do have to come back, otherwise pauses become a way of burying topics.

A line for the pause

"I'm boiling over and I don't want to say something I'll regret. Twenty minutes, and I'll come back. I promise."
chat: We started with him being late and ended up on my mother and his salary. Same as always.
That's topic pile-up: three more grievances got stuck to one, and now neither of you can settle any of them. The hottest one probably isn't the lateness.
Try going back to a single topic and starting with yourself: I was hurt sitting there waiting. We'll talk about the rest separately, I promise.
try: If the fight already broke every rule

It happens. Tell Mediator what went on, each of you privately, from your own side. The bot helps you both see what actually happened and suggests a way to talk about it that doesn't turn into round two. The first analysis is free.
after:
Rule 5. One fight, one topic

A fight about being late shouldn't pick up last year's vacation, your mother and "well, back in 2022 you..." along the way. Every topic you glue on doubles the heat and halves the odds of settling anything. The rule is simple and hard to hold, so say it out loud: "Stop, that's a different subject. Let's finish this one first."

Rule 6. The repair matters more than the fight

In strong couples there is a second act after the conflict: making up for real, not as a formality. Apologizing for the delivery even when you were right on the substance. Saying out loud what each of you understood. Agreeing on what you'll do differently. A skipped repair leaves a crack, and the next fight will run straight along it. We wrote out how to do the repair step by step in the piece on making up after a big fight.

A quick check: did you fight fair last time?

  • Did it start with "I feel" or with "you always"?
  • Were you talking about the act, or did it turn personal?
  • Was there contempt: smirks, eye rolls, mimicking?
  • Did you stop before the shouting, or during it?
  • Was there one topic, or did five get glued together?
  • Was there a repair afterward, or did it just fade out?

Two or more bad answers means the technique is limping. That is fixable, and faster than you'd think. The rules are simple, and a few weeks of paying attention is usually enough.
faq: What if I am the only one following the rules?

Start anyway. A fight is a dance for two, and when one person stops advancing, the other quickly runs out of anyone to battle. A calm "it matters to me that we talk without shouting, let's try" turns out to be contagious over time.
How do you stop a fight before it turns into shouting?

Catch the moment your body speeds up: heart going, voice climbing, the urge to interrupt. That is the point to call the pause out loud and name when you will come back. Twenty minutes is the usual minimum, and it works far better than trying to win while flooded.
We never fight at all. Is that a good sign?

Depends what's under the hood. If you genuinely talk everything through calmly, wonderful. If one of you just stays quiet and stockpiles it, the quiet is deceptive: unsaid things tend to detonate later and louder.

card: AI mediator for couples: how the format actually works
title: AI mediator for couples: how it works, who it helps
desc: What mediation for a couple is, how the shuttle format differs from a shared chat with a therapist, and why telling your side privately is safer in a hot fight.
h1: AI mediator for couples: how it works and who it helps
alt: A neutral mediator on a phone screen holding two threads that lead to two people with phones
tldr: Shuttle mediation: the go-between listens to each side alone and carries over the substance, not the words.
The bot does the same in Telegram: a private analysis for each of you, lines to open with, a shared ending.
It does not replace a therapist and says so plainly when you need a person.
body:
When a couple is in a fight, both people are usually stuck in the same place. Talking to each other has stopped working, because every attempt slides into round two. A couples therapist is slow, expensive, and good luck talking the other person into it. Meanwhile you need to say it out loud and figure out what to do today, ideally before the hurt sets. An AI mediator for couples is built for exactly that gap.

Here is where the format comes from, how it works, and how it differs from just asking a chatbot.

What shuttle mediation is

Professional mediators have a technique for conflicts where the sides aren't ready to sit face to face yet. The go-between moves between them, hears each one alone, and passes on not the words but the substance, with the poison strained out. It is called shuttle diplomacy, and it has been working since long before anyone tried it on couples.

Mediator moves that technique into Telegram. Each of you writes your version of the fight to the bot in private. Angry, hurt, exactly as it is: the other person never sees it. Then the bot prepares a separate personal analysis for each of you: what happened, what feelings and needs are sitting under your reaction, how your particular way of defending yourself keeps the fight going, and what small step would take the heat down. About the other side it offers only careful guesses. It never retells or quotes their words.

Why privacy is the whole point here

In the hot stage of a fight, putting two people in one chat is risky even when the moderator is artificial. Every line written in front of an opponent is written to win, not to be understood. A private format removes the audience. When nobody is watching, people stop composing accusations remarkably fast and start talking about what actually hurts.

What an AI mediator for couples can actually do

  • Break down the fight for each of you separately, using the approaches family therapists work with, the Gottman method among them.
  • Suggest the first lines for the conversation and one concrete step for the next few days.
  • Rewrite a sharp message into a calm one before you send it.
  • Close the topic together when you are both ready: each of you says where you landed, and the bot writes one shared ending.
  • Come back the next day and ask whether the conversation happened. And notice when the same topic keeps coming around.

What it doesn't do, and doesn't pretend to: it is not a therapist, not a judge, and it can't repair a relationship where there is abuse or where one person decided long ago. In those situations the bot says plainly that you need a human being, and points you to help.

How it differs from asking ChatGPT

The main difference is the number of sides. An ordinary chatbot hears only you, so it almost always agrees. You told your version, in your version you are right, and an agreeable assistant confirms it. That feels good and leads nowhere near peace. Sometimes it makes things worse: certainty is excellent fuel for the next round.

Mediator hears both sides and by design takes neither. Its job isn't to hand down a verdict, it's to get two people to finally hear each other.
chat: We haven't spoken in a week after a fight about his mother. He thinks I went too far.
You're both describing the same evening, but different things hurt. For you, that he didn't take your side. For him, that you were sharp about his family. Both of those are real.
You could start somewhere other than who was right: I felt alone when you said nothing. And I know bringing your mom into it was too much.
try: Trying it is easier than reading about it

The first analysis is free. Start a session, tell your side, and your partner joins by your link in about ten seconds, with nothing to install. If they aren't ready yet, start on your own: the figure it out myself mode exists for that.

Who the format suits

  • Couples right after a specific fight, while the hurt is fresh and both of you are still wound up.
  • People whose one topic has been repeating for months, where every conversation about it turns into shouting.
  • Anyone getting ready for a hard conversation who wants to walk in composed.
  • Anyone who isn't ready to sit in a therapist's office yet but does want to understand what is going on.

And one honest note. If your fights come with fear, threats or a sense that home isn't safe, start with real people rather than a bot. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is free, confidential and open around the clock, and if you are in danger, call your local emergency number (911 in the US).
faq: Will my partner see my messages?

No. Each of you writes to the bot privately. The other side sees only a careful, general read of how you might be feeling, with no quotes and no retelling. Sessions delete themselves after a week, and you can wipe everything with one tap in the menu at any moment.
Is an AI mediator a replacement for couples therapy?
No. It is first aid in a conflict and preparation for a conversation. The bot doesn't play therapist, and on serious topics it tells you to go see one.
How much does an AI mediator cost?

The first analysis is free. After that it is a subscription: 250 Telegram Stars for 30 days. Stars are bought in a couple of taps inside Telegram with a card from any country. Only one of you pays, and your partner joins for free.
